title: In The Drops: Rapha’s David Carson kit, Breitling’s Eddy Merckx watch, Povec electrochromic glasses, For a Yellow Jersey book and pubs
content:
Cyclist
In The Drops: Rapha’s David Carson kit, Breitling’s Eddy Merckx watch, Povec electrochromic glasses, For a Yellow Jersey book and pubs

The Premier League is back, the sun sets at 7pm, schoolkids are back at school and the Tube is rammed at 8am once again. That can only mean one thing. It’s the first week of September.

In pro cycling terms, it also means we’re heading towards the end of another season. The Vuelta a España has lit up in the past week since the departure from the race of Tadej Pogačar. On the website, we’ve been keeping an eye on the podium race, while Robyn Davidson poured fuel on the Enric Mas fire that seems to be engulfing Spain right now. With a full week of the Vuelta still left, all is still to play for though. How exciting.

It’s been a busy week for tech releases too. This morning, Factor released its latest gravel bike, the Elara. Spoiler: it looks awfully similar to a Factor One, but with fatter tyres and chunkier chainstays. The British brand wasn’t alone this week, as Pinarello and Scott also unveiled new releases, with the updated Addict Gravel and Dogma X Series.

With that covered, it’s time to get In The Drops.

Rapha x David Carson kit

After collaborations with Palace, Patta and Paul Smith in recent years, Rapha has unveiled its latest limited range, this time with American graphic designer David Carson.

Carson is known for his uniquely chaotic blend of colour, typography and collage-like designs. That earned him the title of ‘the reigning Picasso of the graphic design community’, according to Graphis magazine last year.

Now he’s taken his bold style to Lycra as part of his second collection for UK-based brand Rapha. The 2026 collection includes Carson-ified jerseys, a roadsuit, gilet, cargo bib shorts and accessories, alongside T-shirts, a hoodie and cap.

Every piece in the range is said to channel ‘Carson’s raw, untamed spirit’ through the use of ‘cloud and sky motifs emblematic of unrestricted thought’. Rapha continue to say that ‘these repeated ideas bang the drum for “doing’” without worrying where the journey might take you’. 

In the jersey and bib combination I’ve been sporting, those blue tones stand out, as do the pop art-style hands reaching out across the back panel of the jersey. This jersey, which follows the brand’s usual Rouleur Jersey, is paired nicely with a brown pair of cargo bib shorts with the word ‘Freedom’ etched onto the left leg.

If you want a bigger splash of colour, the skinsuits on offer in the Carson x Rapha range feature every shade under the sun on a long-sleeve garment. Go on, give it a look on the Rapha website.

  • Explore the full range from Rapha

Povec C1 electrochromic sunglasses

Move over, cycling sunnies with cameras and Bluetooth speakers built in. New smart eyewear brand Povec claim its C1 sunglasses to be the first solid-state electrochromic lenses on the market. Let’s break that down.

Photochromic glasses use a technology that allows the lens to adapt its clarity to the surrounding light. Traditional photochromic lenses can take 20–60 seconds to adapt. In order to speed up that transition, Povec has developed an electrochromic solution.

This means the C1 sunnies use an electric system to allow you to change the lenses near instantly with the swipe of a finger at the glasses’ temple. That swipe swaps the lenses between Category 2 (37% VLT) and Category 3 (9% VLT) lenses.

This tech makes for much quicker adaptation to light when your ride switches between bright sunlight and shade, like riding under tree cover or through tunnels. All it takes is a swipe, not too dissimilar to the one you make on your AirPods to skip a song.

The glasses are powered by a battery that is claimed to offer enough power for up to 28 days of usage. Don’t worry, the electronics are also weather-resistant, with an official IP65 rating that means it’s been tested against the heaviest of downpours and wind.

Despite the battery system, the glasses are still lightweight, at a claimed 36g. The lenses also come with considerable UV protection, at UV400.

  • Available from Povec ($249)

Breitling Top Time Eddy Merckx watch

At the Tour de France, you might have spotted a certain Paul Seixas sporting a leather-strapped, yellow-faced watch. That was the Breitling Top Time B01 Chronograph 41 Eddy Merckx watch.

The timepiece was launched the week of the Tour’s Grand Départ in Barcelona in celebration of the sport’s greatest rider. Yes, Eddy Merckx is referenced all over this watch, with an ‘Eddy Merckx Tribute’ is written on the open caseback, and a signature at 6 o’clock. 

There are some parallels to Merckx’s career. The Top Time collection was introduced in the 1960s, when Merckx began his career. There’s also a yellow watch face in homage to the Belgian’s record-equalling five Tour victories.

The 41mm watch’s power comes from Breitling’s Manufacture Caliber 01, an automatic chronograph movement with COSC certification and a 70-hour power reserve. It’s offered with either a calfskin leather strap or a stainless steel mesh bracelet.

The Merckx watch is on a limited run of 525 units. That’s precisely the number of victories Merckx claimed during his career, including his five Tour wins, five Giro titles and three world titles on the road. There are still some to go around, so you too could be part of an elite club alongside Merckx and Seixas.

However, if that’s got your Merckx senses tingling, keep an eye out for an upcoming interview with the man behind the watch in an upcoming issue of our magazine.

  • Available from Breitling (£6,200)

For A Yellow Jersey by Paul Maunder

Since my last In The Drops, I’ve been to both the Tour de France Femmes and the Tour of Britain Women. In preparation for the big races, I chomped through Paul Maunder’s book titled For A Yellow Jersey.

The book, claimed to be the first comprehensive work on the history of the women’s Tour, charts the rise, fall and rise again of the women’s Tour de France throughout the decades. The story starts out in the 1950s in order to chart the turbulent history of the event, which was plagued by mismanagement blunders, financial mishandling and countless missed opportunities.

There are exclusive interviews and quotes from riders past and present in the book, plus notable team staff, race directors and the key figures behind every iteration of the women’s Tour de France. Even the one-day La Course event.

  • Available from Waterstones (£25)

What we’re into this week: Going to the pub

I’ll be honest, I haven’t really been up to much this week apart from riding my bike, going to the pub and spending too much money on food over the past few weeks.

In that case, here’s a list of London boozers I’ve enjoyed over the past month or so.

  • Le Beaujolais, Soho
  • The Alma, Newington Green
  • The Robin, Crouch Hill
  • Fultering Fullback, Finsbury Park
  • The Shakespeare, Stoke Newington
  • The Scolt Head, De Beauvoir
  • Rutland Arms, Hammersmith
  • Lord Clyde, Southwark
